title: In every heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaakur, and your line: lord of all. The circle widened to every living thing; today it moves inward, to the heart.

A subway car at rush hour. Forty strangers, shoulder to shoulder, all carefully not looking at one another. A man in a suit reading his phone. A teenager with headphones and eyes closed. A grandmother with grocery bags, a nurse just off a night shift. Each face closed, like a house with the curtains drawn. You could ride with them every day for a year and never know one name. The twenty-second ashtpadi makes a claim about every one of those closed houses: someone lives inside.
screen: `FORTY STRANGERS, NOT LOOKING.` → `EACH FACE A CLOSED HOUSE.` → `SOMEONE LIVES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the One is spread through all beings. The twenty-second ashtpadi presses the point home: God dwells in every heart, ghat ghat, in each body and each being. Ghat literally means a pot or vessel, a clay jar. Gurbani uses it for the body, and for the heart inside it, the way a jar holds water. Doubled, ghat ghat means in every single one. Gurbani returns to this again and again. In Sohila, the prayer before sleep, Guru Nanak sings, in paraphrase: within all is the Light, and You are that Light; by its shining, everything shines. Every face on that subway car is a clay jar with the same Light inside. This is the ground under some very practical things Sikhs do. It's why the langar, the free kitchen, seats everyone on the floor in the same rows, whoever they are. It's why the Gurus spoke so sharply against treating people as high or low by caste. And it's why, for Sikhs, seva, serving others, is never only charity: if the Light is in every heart, serving a stranger is serving the One who lives there. It's a demanding teaching. It's easy to see the Light in a smiling child or a kind friend, and harder in the man who shoved past you for a seat. Sukhmani makes no exception for him. Ghat ghat means every jar.
screen: `GHAT GHAT: IN EVERY VESSEL.` · `THE SAME LIGHT IN EACH.` · `THE GROUND UNDER LANGAR AND SEVA.` · `NO EXCEPTIONS, EVEN THE RUDE ONE.` · then, large: `EVERY HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary face, not your favorite person in the world, or look at one nearby or in a photo, and take in the eyes, the lines, the expression. Hold the thought, there's Light in this jar too, and if that comes easily, try a harder face. If you pray, say Waheguru softly as you look.
Ghat ghat, in every vessel: Sukhmani says God dwells in every vessel, every body and heart, and Sohila adds that the same Light shines in all.
Your line: every heart. Each face on the train, the same Light inside. Same time tomorrow.

chat.says: Do Sikhs really believe God is in everyone? Even rude people?
options: Sukhmani says God dwells ghat ghat, in every heart, so yes, even the rude one has that Light.
Only in good and gentle hearts; the Light leaves anyone who acts badly toward others.
Not really; the Light is only in the gurdwara, so you meet it when you go there.
